items.prompt: What is the main job of a load balancer in a system design?

options.label: Split a large table into smaller pieces by key
Hold messages until a worker can process them
Spread incoming requests across several servers
Store query results in memory for faster reads

rubric: A load balancer distributes traffic across servers.
Distractors describe a cache, a queue and sharding.

items.prompt: Which component is typically used to keep frequently read data in memory to reduce database load?

options.label: Cache
Message queue
Load balancer
Firewall

rubric: A cache keeps hot data in fast memory.
A queue buffers work and does not speed up reads.

items.prompt: What does 'horizontal scaling' mean?

options.label: Adding more CPU and RAM to one machine
Moving servers into a different region
Adding more machines to share the work
Copying data to a backup once a day

rubric: Horizontal scaling adds more machines.
The second option is vertical scaling.

items.prompt: What is a message queue used for?

options.label: Encrypting traffic between client and server
Buffering messages between producers and consumers
Translating domain names to IP addresses
Enforcing foreign keys in a relational table

rubric: Queues decouple producers from consumers by buffering messages.
Other options describe TLS, DNS and database constraints.

items.prompt: What does 'single point of failure' mean?

options.label: A component whose failure stops the whole system
A user who sends all requests from one IP address
A database table with only one column
A server that handles only one request at a time

rubric: A SPOF is a component whose failure takes the system down.
Distractors confuse it with concurrency or unrelated single-item ideas.

items.prompt: Which of the following are common techniques for scaling a database for reads or size? Select all that apply.

options.label: Adding more comments to code
Read replicas
Sharding
Renaming columns

rubric: Replicas spread reads and sharding splits data across nodes.
Comments and renaming do not change capacity.

items.prompt: A team is drawing the architecture for a photo-sharing app. They need a place to store large image files cheaply, separate from the relational database holding user records. Which kind of component fits storing the image files?

options.label: A message queue
A load balancer
A DNS server
An object store

rubric: Object storage suits large binary files.
Queues, load balancers and DNS do not store files.

items.prompt: Why do designers often put a cache in front of a database?

options.label: Repeated reads are served from fast memory, so the database does less work
It guarantees data is never out of date
It removes the need to back up the database
It lets the database accept writes without storing them

rubric: Caches cut read load and latency.
Caches can serve stale data and do not replace storage.

items.prompt: Why is a queue useful between a web server and a slow email-sending job?

options.label: It makes each email send faster on the worker
It encrypts the emails before sending
It guarantees emails arrive in the inbox
The web server can reply quickly while emails are sent later

rubric: Queues decouple slow work from the request path.
A queue does not speed up the work itself or guarantee delivery.

items.prompt: What is the main benefit of running two copies of a service behind a load balancer?

options.label: Each request is processed twice for accuracy
If one copy fails, the other can keep serving requests
The service uses less memory overall
Database queries become unnecessary

rubric: Redundancy improves availability.
Requests are not duplicated; memory use rises.

items.prompt: Which statement best explains vertical versus horizontal scaling?

options.label: Vertical is for databases only; horizontal is for caches only
Vertical adds machines; horizontal makes one machine bigger
Vertical and horizontal both mean copying data to backups
Vertical makes one machine bigger; horizontal adds more machines

rubric: Vertical means bigger machine; horizontal means more machines.
The first option swaps the definitions.

items.prompt: What is a drawback of caching data?

options.label: Reads become slower than hitting the database
Caches cannot hold more than one item
Caches need a message queue to work
Cached data can become stale after the source changes

rubric: Stale data is the key cache trade-off.
Caches speed reads and hold many items.

items.prompt: Which are reasons to add database read replicas? Select all that apply.

options.label: Keep serving reads if the primary is slow or down
Spread read traffic across more servers
Make every write faster
Remove the need for any indexes

rubric: Replicas add read capacity and some resilience.
Writes still go to the primary; indexes remain useful.

items.prompt: A small shop's website runs on one server and crashes when a sale brings heavy traffic. The team adds three more identical servers and a load balancer in front. What does this change mainly achieve?

options.label: It lets the site handle more traffic and survive a server failure
It stops customers from seeing old prices
It removes the need to store orders
It makes the database schema normalized

rubric: More servers plus a load balancer add capacity and redundancy.
It does not address schema, stale data or storage.

items.prompt: Why does adding a cache such as Redis in front of the database help a read-heavy product catalog?

options.label: Cached data is always identical to the database, so the database no longer needs to store it durably
Caches make writes faster than the database, so the database can be dropped from the write path
A cache keeps data consistent across all replicas, so users never see outdated product details
Repeated reads are served from fast memory, cutting latency and database load

rubric: A cache answers repeated reads from memory, which lowers latency and database load.
Distractors assume caches are always consistent or replace durable storage, which they do not.

items.prompt: What is the main job of a load balancer placed in front of several identical web servers?

options.label: It stores user data on each server so that the servers stay in sync with the database
It encrypts all traffic so the servers no longer need to handle any security checks themselves
It spreads incoming requests across healthy servers so none is overloaded
It speeds up each query by rewriting SQL statements before they reach the database tier

rubric: A load balancer distributes requests across healthy servers.
Distractors confuse it with data sync, security tooling or a query optimiser.

items.prompt: An order service publishes 'order placed' messages to a queue, and an email service consumes them. What does the queue mainly provide?

options.label: Decoupling, so orders are still accepted when the email service is slow or down
Synchronous replies so the order service can read the email result before it answers the user
Guaranteed delivery of each email to the customer's inbox within a fixed deadline set by the queue
Automatic sharding of the orders table across every database used by both of the services

rubric: A queue decouples producer and consumer so one can be slow or down without blocking the other.
Distractors credit the queue with delivery deadlines, sharding or synchronous replies, none of which it gives.

items.prompt: A site slows down as traffic grows. Which change is an example of horizontal scaling?

options.label: Adding a larger disk to the database server to hold more rows
Rewriting a slow function so it uses fewer CPU cycles per request
Upgrading the single server to one with more CPU cores and memory
Adding more identical servers behind a load balancer to share traffic

rubric: Horizontal scaling adds more machines to share the load.
Bigger hardware is vertical scaling, and code optimisation is neither.

items.prompt: A user updates their profile, and the next page load reads from a read replica that is a few seconds behind the primary. What will most likely happen?

options.label: The page may show the old profile, because the replica has not yet received the update
The primary rejects the update until every replica has confirmed that it has applied the change
The page fails with an error because replicas refuse reads for a user who has just written
The replica pushes its older copy back to the primary and overwrites the newly written profile

rubric: Asynchronous replication lag means replicas can return stale data right after a write.
Distractors invent replica-to-primary overwrites or write blocking, which do not occur in standard replication.

items.prompt: Which statements explain why keeping web servers stateless makes scaling easier? Select all that apply.

options.label: Stateless servers never need a database, since all data lives in the client browser
Any server can handle any request, so a load balancer can send traffic anywhere
Stateless servers cannot fail, so health checks are no longer required
Servers can be added or removed without losing per-user data held in their memory

rubric: With no local state, requests can go to any server and servers can come and go freely.
Stateless does not mean no database or no failures; state just lives in a shared store.

items.prompt: A photo app resizes each uploaded image inside the upload request. On busy evenings uploads take 20 seconds and some time out. The team proposes saving the original, putting a resize job on a queue, and returning success immediately. Why does this fix the timeouts?

options.label: Returning success early guarantees that the resized image is already available when the user opens it
The queue compresses the original image so that it uploads faster over the user's network connection
Resizing leaves the request path, so users wait only for the save while workers resize later
The queue makes resizing itself faster by running each image's pixel work in parallel inside the queue

rubric: Moving slow work to background workers shortens the request and absorbs spikes.
Distractors assume the queue speeds up compute or guarantees immediate availability of the result.

items.prompt: An app has 10 million daily active users, each making 10 requests per day spread evenly over 24 hours. About how many requests per second is that on average?

options.label: About 115
About 1,150
About 115,000
About 11,500

rubric: 10^8 requests divided by 86,400 seconds is about 1,150 per second.
Other options come from slipping a factor of ten when dividing by seconds per day.

items.prompt: A service stores 1 million new records per day, each about 2 KB. Roughly how much new storage is needed per year, ignoring replication?

options.label: About 7.3 TB
About 73 GB
About 73 TB
About 730 GB

rubric: 2 KB times 1 million is 2 GB per day, and times 365 is about 730 GB.
Other options are order-of-magnitude slips in units or multiplication.

items.prompt: Using the cache-aside pattern, a request for product 42 misses the cache. Which sequence does the application follow?

options.label: Write product 42 to the cache first, then read it back from the database to verify
Read product 42 from the database, store it in the cache, then return it
Return an empty result, then have the cache fetch product 42 from the database later
Ask the database to update the cache itself, then return whatever the cache holds

rubric: In cache-aside the application loads from the database on a miss, populates the cache, then returns the data.
Distractors give the cache or database responsibilities that belong to the application in this pattern.

items.prompt: A payments service must debit one account and credit another so that both changes happen or neither does. Which storage choice fits best?

options.label: A message queue that applies the debit and credit independently
A CDN that replicates the balances to edge locations
A relational database with one transaction around both updates
A cache with a short TTL that holds both balances in memory

rubric: A relational transaction gives all-or-nothing atomicity across both updates.
Caches, independent queue consumers and CDNs give no atomic multi-row guarantee.

items.prompt: An orders table is split across 8 shards. Most queries fetch all orders for one customer, and customers order at similar rates. Which shard key fits best?

options.label: Order creation date, so recent orders sit together on one shard
Hash of customer_id, so a customer's orders share a shard and load spreads evenly
Customer country, so orders from each region stay on their own shard
Random value per order, so each shard gets the same number of rows

rubric: Hashing customer_id keeps one customer's orders together and spreads load evenly.
Date creates hot shards, country skews load, and random keys force queries across all shards.

items.prompt: A flash sale will send 50 times the usual read traffic to product pages that change rarely. Which measures reduce database load? Select all that apply.

options.label: Cache product pages in memory with a short TTL
Add read replicas and route product reads to them
Have every request bypass the cache to get fresh data
Add an index on every column of the orders table

rubric: Caching and read replicas absorb repeated reads for rarely changing data.
Extra indexes slow writes without helping this load, and bypassing the cache increases database traffic.

items.prompt: A web app runs on three servers behind a load balancer, with login sessions stored in each server's memory. Users report being randomly logged out after a few clicks. Which change fixes this while keeping three servers?

options.label: Add a fourth server so each user is less likely to land on a new machine
Move sessions to a shared store such as Redis that all three servers read
Switch the load balancer to random routing so each user's requests are mixed evenly
Increase each server's memory so that sessions survive longer between requests

rubric: Sessions held in one server's memory are missing when the next request lands elsewhere; a shared store fixes this.
Adding memory or servers, or randomising routing, does not make session data available to every server.

items.prompt: A service has 10 million daily active users, and each user makes 20 requests per day on average. Assuming traffic is spread evenly over 24 hours (86,400 seconds), what is the average request rate?

options.label: About 2,300 requests per second
About 200,000 requests per second
About 230 requests per second
About 23,000 requests per second

rubric: 10M x 20 = 200M requests/day; divided by about 86,400 seconds gives roughly 2,300 per second.
Distractors come from misplacing a power of ten when dividing by seconds per day.

items.prompt: You implement a cache-aside read path for a user profile lookup. Which sequence of steps is correct?

options.label: Write to the cache and database on every read so the two stay identical, then return the cached value
Check the cache; on a miss, read the database, store the result in the cache, then return it
Query the database first, then write the result to the cache, and only check the cache on the next request
Check the cache; on a miss, return an empty result and let a background job fill the cache later

rubric: Cache-aside checks the cache, falls back to the database on a miss, and populates the cache before returning.
Distractors skip the cache check or confuse reads with write-through behaviour.

items.prompt: A photo app receives 5 million new photos per day, averaging 2 MB each. Photos are kept for 1 year and every object is stored with 3 replicas. Roughly how much raw storage is needed?

options.label: About 1.2 PB
About 36 PB
About 3.7 PB
About 11 PB

rubric: 5M x 2 MB = 10 TB/day; x 365 = about 3.65 PB; x 3 replicas = about 11 PB.
3.7 PB forgets replication; the others are arithmetic or unit slips.

items.prompt: An orders table must be sharded across 8 databases. Nearly all queries fetch or insert orders for a single user, and traffic should spread evenly. Which shard key fits best?

options.label: Country code, so regional users share a shard and queries stay local
Order creation date, so recent orders are grouped together on one shard
Hash of user_id, so each user's orders sit on one shard and users spread evenly
Order status, so open orders are separated from completed ones

rubric: Hashing user_id keeps single-user queries on one shard and distributes load evenly.
Date, country and status keys cause hot shards and uneven or shifting distribution.

items.prompt: A token bucket rate limiter has capacity 10 and refills 2 tokens per second; it starts full. A client sends 15 requests at t=0, then 5 more requests at t=1.5s. How many requests are allowed in total?
rubric: At t=0 only 10 tokens exist, so 10 pass; by t=1.5s, 3 tokens have refilled, so 3 of the 5 pass: 13.
Distractors ignore the refill or the bucket's capacity.

items.prompt: A queue gives at-least-once delivery to a consumer that creates shipping labels, so duplicates can occur. Which measures make the consumer safe to retry? Select all that apply.

options.label: Record processed message IDs and skip any ID already seen
Acknowledge the message on receipt so it is never redelivered
Acknowledge the message only after the label is saved successfully
Disable producer retries so duplicates cannot be sent
Write labels with an upsert keyed by order ID so repeats do not create copies

rubric: Deduplication, idempotent writes and ack-after-success make redelivery harmless.
Acking on receipt risks losing work on a crash, and disabling retries trades duplicates for lost messages.

items.prompt: A web app runs on three servers behind a round-robin load balancer. Login sessions are kept in each server's local memory, and users are randomly logged out as requests land on different servers. The team wants to keep round-robin and avoid sticky routing. What should they do?

options.label: Shorten the session timeout so stale sessions clear sooner
Increase each server's memory so sessions survive longer in local storage
Store sessions in a shared store such as Redis that every server reads and writes
Add a fourth server so fewer requests land on any one server

rubric: A shared session store makes servers stateless, so any server can handle any request.
The other options do not make session data visible across servers.

items.prompt: After a deploy, a cache's hit ratio fell from 92% to near 0% and database load tripled. The diff shows the cache key was changed to `user:{id}:{request_timestamp_ms}`. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: The database became slower, which makes cached entries expire sooner
The cache's TTL was set too low relative to the read traffic
The key now includes a value unique to each request, so no key is ever reused
The cache ran out of memory and began evicting entries too quickly

rubric: A per-request timestamp in the key means every lookup is a new key and always misses.
Eviction, TTL and DB speed would not drop hit ratio to near zero immediately after this change.

items.prompt: Users update their profile, are redirected to the profile page, and sometimes see old values; a refresh seconds later shows the new ones. Writes go to the primary and reads go to replicas. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: The replica serving the read has not yet applied the write because of replication lag
The browser cache is set to ignore server responses for profile pages
The primary database rejected the write and silently retried it later
The load balancer is dropping the write request on some connections

rubric: Asynchronous replication means a replica can briefly lag, so read-after-write may return stale data.
If writes were lost, a later refresh would not show new values.

items.prompt: Checkout calls the email provider synchronously after payment. When the provider slows down, checkout p99 latency climbs and timeouts increase, though payment itself is healthy. What does this analysis show?

options.label: The database has too many connections open during payments
Checkout needs a CDN in front of it to absorb the slow responses
The email call sits in the request path, so provider slowness is passed on to checkout
Payment processing is the bottleneck and needs more capacity

rubric: A synchronous dependency couples checkout latency to the email provider; a queue would decouple them.
Payment is stated to be healthy, and a CDN does not help dynamic backend calls.

items.prompt: A multi-tenant system shards data by hash(tenant_id) across 10 shards. One shard runs at 95% CPU while the others sit near 20%. One tenant generates about 40% of all traffic. What explains the imbalance?

options.label: Hash-based sharding always concentrates writes on the first shard
The hash function is biased and must be replaced with a stronger one
There are too few shards, so adding more would split that tenant
All of a tenant's data maps to one shard, so a very heavy tenant creates a hotspot

rubric: Skew is in the key's access distribution, not the hash; a single tenant maps to one shard.
Adding shards or changing the hash does not split one tenant's traffic.

items.prompt: Service A (own availability 99.99%) must call both service B (99.9%) and service C (99.9%) on every request, with no fallback. Failures are independent. What is A's approximate end-to-end availability?
rubric: Serial dependencies multiply: 0.9999 x 0.999 x 0.999 is about 0.9979.
99.99% ignores dependencies; 99.69% overcounts the loss.

items.prompt: A team doubled the number of stateless app servers, but throughput stayed flat. Which findings could explain this? Select all that apply.

options.label: The new servers use a different operating system patch level
Every request takes a global distributed lock, which serialises the work
The load balancer uses IP hashing, and most traffic comes via one corporate proxy IP
The database is already at maximum CPU, so extra app servers just queue on it
The app servers are stateless, so they cannot handle more traffic

rubric: A saturated shared resource, a serialising lock, or skewed routing each cap throughput regardless of server count.
Statelessness helps scaling, and a patch level does not by itself cap throughput.

items.prompt: A very popular product page is cached with a 60-second TTL. Every minute, database CPU spikes briefly and page latency jumps, then it recovers. Cache hit ratio is otherwise 99%. Which analysis best explains the pattern?

options.label: When the key expires, many concurrent requests miss at once and all query the database
Network latency between app and cache rises periodically on the minute
The database runs a scheduled backup each minute that competes with queries
The cache evicts the key early because memory is nearly full

rubric: The spike aligns with TTL expiry: a cache stampede sends many simultaneous misses to the database.
Eviction or network issues would not produce a regular 60-second pattern tied to the TTL.

items.prompt: After a deploy, a product-page cache hit ratio falls from 95% to 20% while database load triples. The only change adds a `?session_id=...` tracking parameter to every page URL, and the cache key is the full URL. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: The cache is too small, so entries are evicted before they are reused
Every user now generates a unique key, so repeat requests for the same page miss
The database is slower, so entries are expiring earlier than their TTL
The tracking parameter increased payload size, which disables caching of large pages

rubric: Including a per-user value in the key fragments one page into many keys, so hits collapse.
Capacity and TTL explanations don't fit a sudden drop tied to a key change.

items.prompt: A user edits their display name, the page reloads, and the old name appears for a few seconds before the new one shows. Writes go to a primary, and reads go to asynchronous replicas. Which diagnosis best fits?

options.label: Replication lag lets a replica serve the read before it has applied the write
The replicas use a weaker isolation level, which blocks the write for seconds
The browser cache served an old response because the database lacked indexes
The primary rolled back the write, which was re-applied later by a retry

rubric: Asynchronous replication means a replica can lag the primary, breaking read-your-writes.
Isolation level and rollback explanations don't produce a transient stale read that self-heals.

items.prompt: A queue consumer charges customers and acknowledges the message after the charge. Some customers are charged twice after a consumer crash. The broker guarantees at-least-once delivery. Which analysis is correct?

options.label: The queue should use more partitions, since partitions cause duplicate delivery
Acknowledging after processing is the flaw, because acking first would prevent all loss and duplicates
The broker has a bug that delivers messages twice during normal operation
Crashing after the charge but before the ack causes redelivery of a non-idempotent handler

rubric: A crash between the side effect and the ack triggers redelivery; the handler needs idempotency.
Acking first trades duplicates for possible loss; it doesn't fix the problem.

items.prompt: A time-series events table is sharded by day, with each day's range on a different shard. Ingest is steady, yet one shard hits CPU limits while the others sit idle. What explains this?

options.label: The idle shards hold too much old data, which blocks inserts on the busy one
The newest shard has more indexes than the others, which makes inserts slower
Range sharding on a monotonic key sends all current writes to the newest shard
Hash sharding would have caused the same hotspot, since the writes are all inserts

rubric: Monotonic range keys concentrate all new writes on one shard.
Index count and old-data explanations don't account for the skew between shards.

items.prompt: A service fans out each request to 40 backends in parallel and waits for all. Each backend has a p99 latency of 100 ms and a median of 5 ms. Users see slow responses on a large share of requests. What is the best analysis?

options.label: The median of the backends is too high, so average latency drives the slowness
The chance that at least one of 40 calls hits its slow tail is high, so the tail dominates
Parallel calls add up their latencies, so the total is about 40 times the median
The network between services is saturated, which is the only cause of waiting for all

rubric: Waiting on all calls means one slow call delays the request; with 40 calls about 1-0.99^40 ≈ 33% see a tail hit.
Parallel latency is the maximum, not the sum, which rules out the additive explanation.

items.prompt: A popular cached key expires and the database is overwhelmed by thousands of identical recomputation queries at once. Which factors contribute to this stampede? Select all that apply.

options.label: No request coalescing or lock exists to let one request refill the key
Many requests find the key missing at the same moment and all recompute it
The cache uses LRU eviction, which always evicts popular keys first
The recomputation is expensive relative to what the database can handle concurrently

rubric: A stampede needs simultaneous misses, costly recomputation, and no coalescing.
LRU tends to keep popular keys, so it isn't a cause here.

items.prompt: A web tier uses a load balancer with sticky sessions (cookie lifetime 24 hours). Autoscaling adds 6 new instances during a traffic spike, yet CPU on the 4 original instances stays at 90% while the new ones sit at 10%. Traffic from existing users continues. What explains this?

options.label: Sticky cookies keep returning users on their original instances, so new instances get only new users
The new instances fail health checks intermittently and are taken out of rotation
The load balancer uses least-connections, which always favours the oldest instances
Autoscaling adds instances with smaller CPU capacity, so they report lower utilisation

rubric: Sticky sessions pin existing users to their instances, so new capacity only serves new sessions.
Health-check and instance-size explanations aren't suggested by the symptoms; the original instances stay saturated.

items.prompt: A ticketing system must never oversell seats, can accept 200 ms extra latency on checkout, and has one region. Which approach best meets these criteria?

options.label: Use eventually consistent replicas for seat counts, with a nightly job fixing oversells
Let each web server track its own seat quota and sync quotas every minute
Decrement the seat count in a single transactional database row with a conditional update
Cache seat counts at the edge and reconcile oversold seats with refunds afterward

rubric: A conditional update in a transactional store enforces the no-oversell invariant within the latency budget.
The other options accept temporary or permanent oversells, which violates the stated criterion.

items.prompt: A product catalogue is read 500 times for every write. Criteria: shoppers must never see a price older than 60 seconds, and write latency matters little. Which cache strategy best fits?

options.label: A 24-hour TTL with a nightly full refresh to reduce database load
No cache, with every read going to the primary to keep prices exact
Cache-aside with a 60-second TTL and explicit invalidation on each price write
Write-behind caching that flushes price changes to the database every few minutes

rubric: A short TTL bounds staleness and invalidation tightens it, while reads stay cheap.
Long TTLs and delayed write-behind violate the 60-second bound; skipping the cache ignores the read-heavy load.

items.prompt: A checkout flow must send a confirmation email after payment. Criteria: email provider outages must not fail the checkout, and no confirmation may be lost. Which design is best?

options.label: Send the email before taking payment so a provider outage is detected early
Call the email provider inline and retry in the request until it succeeds
Fire the email call asynchronously in memory and ignore failures to keep checkout fast
Persist the order and an outbox record in one transaction, then send emails from a queue worker

rubric: The transactional outbox decouples checkout from the provider while retaining durable pending emails.
In-memory fire-and-forget loses messages on a crash, and inline calls couple checkout to the provider.

items.prompt: A banking ledger needs multi-row transfers that are atomic, auditable, and consistent. Volume is 2,000 writes per second, which one well-provisioned node can handle. Which storage choice best meets the criteria?

options.label: A relational database with ACID transactions, replicated for failover
A document store with per-document atomicity and application-side compensation
A key-value store with eventual consistency, partitioned for write scale
An append-only log with consumers deriving balances, without transactions

rubric: ACID transactions give atomic multi-row transfers, and the volume doesn't require giving them up.
The alternatives push atomicity into application code, adding risk without a scale need.

items.prompt: A team proposes enforcing an API rate limit of 100 requests per minute per user by taking a distributed lock in a central store on every request. The API handles 50,000 requests per second across 40 servers. What is the strongest critique?

options.label: The design is sound, since a lock guarantees the exact count at any scale
The limit should be per server rather than per user, which makes locks unnecessary
Locks are only safe for writes, so rate limits can't be counted at all
The central lock serialises every request and adds a latency and availability dependency; atomic counters or local approximations fit better

rubric: A per-request global lock is a throughput and availability bottleneck; atomic increments or approximate local counting are cheaper.
Exactness isn't worth that cost here, and the other options misstate the problem.

items.prompt: A proposal stores all user sessions in one Redis instance with no persistence, to serve a login-required site with 5 million daily users. Which criticisms are valid? Select all that apply.

options.label: A single instance is a single point of failure, so its loss logs everyone out
One node's memory and throughput cap how far sessions can scale
With no persistence, a restart drops every session at once
Redis can't store session data, because it only supports caching

rubric: The single node limits availability, durability and capacity.
Redis is widely used for sessions, so the claim that it cannot store them is wrong.

items.prompt: A chat app must load the latest 50 messages of a conversation quickly. Conversations range from 2 people to 100,000-member channels. Criteria: even write distribution, single-conversation reads hit one shard, and no hot shard from a large channel. Which sharding key is best?

options.label: Sender user ID, which groups a user's messages but splits conversations apart
Conversation ID alone, which keeps reads local but can overload one shard for huge channels
Message ID hash, which spreads writes evenly but scatters each conversation
Conversation ID plus a time bucket, so reads stay local and large channels spread over buckets

rubric: A composite key with a time bucket keeps recent reads local while spreading a big channel's history over shards.
The other keys fail either locality or hotspot criteria.

items.prompt: A ledger service must have an RPO of zero after the loss of any one region, with a write latency budget of 300 ms. Cross-region round trips take about 80 ms. Which replication approach best meets these criteria?

options.label: Nightly snapshots shipped to a second region, plus a write-ahead log archive uploaded every minute
Asynchronous replication to two other regions, accepting seconds of lag so that writes stay fast
Majority-quorum commit across three regions, so each write is durable in two regions before acknowledgement
Synchronous replication to every region, so that all replicas must acknowledge before each write completes

rubric: Quorum commit gives RPO zero with one round trip (~80 ms) inside the budget and survives one region loss.
Async replication loses recent writes; all-region sync lowers availability and ties latency to the slowest region.

items.prompt: A team proposes that every service retry failed calls three times with exponential backoff, claiming this strictly improves reliability. Which critique is most accurate?

options.label: Backoff delays make retries useless, because a failed server has always lost the state of the request
Retries are safe for every operation, so the only real cost is slightly higher latency seen by clients
Exponential backoff synchronises clients, so a fixed short retry interval is always more stable under load
Under overload retries multiply load across layers and sustain the outage unless budgets, jitter and idempotency are added

rubric: Retry amplification across call layers can turn a brief overload into a sustained outage.
Distractors treat retries as free or blame backoff itself.

items.prompt: A multi-tenant SaaS shards by hash(tenant_id). One tenant now produces 40% of traffic and overheats its shard. Queries are always tenant-scoped. Which change best balances load while keeping most queries on one shard?

options.label: Move the large tenant to read replicas on its shard, since read traffic leaving the primary removes the hotspot
Re-hash tenants with a different function, since a better hash will spread the large tenant across all shards
Add a tenant-to-shard directory and split the large tenant over a few dedicated shards by hash(tenant_id, user_id)
Switch to random sharding by row, so each shard gets equal volume even though tenant queries become scatter-gather

rubric: A directory allows targeted placement and bounded splitting of the hot tenant while most tenants stay single-shard.
Re-hashing cannot split one key; row-level sharding loses locality; replicas do not relieve writes.

items.prompt: A service uses a TTL lease lock so only one worker writes to a storage system. A worker stalls in a long GC pause, its lease expires, a second worker takes over, then the first resumes and writes. Which evaluation is correct?

options.label: Unsafe unless storage rejects writes whose fencing token is older than the latest token it has seen
Safe if the TTL is set far above any expected pause, since the lease then can never expire early
Safe, because the worker checked the lock before the write and the pause cannot affect that check
Unsafe only when clocks drift, so NTP synchronisation fully removes the stale-writer problem

rubric: A paused client cannot know its lease expired; only a fencing token checked by the resource guarantees safety.
Longer TTLs and clock sync reduce but never eliminate the race.

items.prompt: An API autoscales on CPU up to 200 instances, each holding a pool of 20 database connections. The database allows 1,000 connections. During a spike, scaling out is followed by rising errors. Which risk assessment ranks highest?

options.label: Scaling out exceeds the database connection limit, so added instances worsen failures; cap instances or pool via a proxy
Instance warm-up time is the main risk, because new instances must load caches before taking requests
Health checks fail on new instances, so they never receive traffic and the spike lands on old instances
CPU is a poor scaling signal, so instances arrive too slowly; switching the metric to memory removes the errors

rubric: 200 x 20 = 4,000 connections exceeds 1,000, so scale-out itself causes the failure.
Other options propose plausible but unsupported causes.

items.prompt: A design keeps shopping carts only in one non-persistent Redis node that also serves as the site's page cache. Requirements: carts survive a node failure, and cache load must not affect carts. Which criticisms are valid? Select all that apply.

options.label: Memory-pressure eviction policies may evict cart keys along with cached pages
Carts must never have a TTL, so any in-memory store is unsuitable
The single node is a single point of failure for all carts
Cache traffic spikes compete with cart operations for the same node's capacity
Redis cannot store structured data such as carts, so a different store is mandatory

rubric: Shared eviction, single point of failure and resource contention each violate a stated requirement.
Redis does store structured data, and carts can have TTLs.

items.prompt: A six-engineer team runs a monolith deployed weekly. Only the image-processing module needs 20x more CPU at peaks, and its crashes occasionally take down checkout. Leadership proposes splitting into 15 microservices. Given the criteria of low operational load and fault isolation, which judgement is best?

options.label: Extract only image processing behind a queue, since it has the distinct load and failure profile, and keep the rest modular
Split by database table, since data ownership boundaries matter more than load profiles when choosing services
Approve the full split, since independent services always give better fault isolation whatever the team size
Reject any change, since weekly deploys show the architecture already meets every current need

rubric: Extracting the one component with a different scaling and failure profile meets both criteria without 15 services of overhead.
Full split overloads a small team; doing nothing ignores the checkout outages.

items.prompt: Design a limit of 10,000 requests/min per API key across 20 edge nodes. Constraints: no remote call on the request path, under 1 ms p99 overhead, and brief overshoot up to 10% is acceptable. Which design meets all constraints?

options.label: Each node holds a local token bucket with a share of the quota, and nodes rebalance shares by exchanging usage asynchronously
Route every request for a key to one node by consistent hashing, then count locally at that node
Each node calls a central counter on every request and rejects once the global count passes the limit
Each node enforces the full 10,000 locally, since evenly spread traffic will make the totals match the limit

rubric: Local buckets with async rebalancing avoid remote calls and keep overshoot bounded.
Central counters and key-affinity routing add a remote hop; full local limits can allow 20x the limit.

items.prompt: Design payment webhook handling on an at-least-once queue so a customer is credited exactly once in effect, even if a worker crashes after crediting but before acknowledging. Which design meets this?

options.label: Run one worker with no concurrency, so duplicates can never be processed at the same time
Insert the event ID under a unique constraint in the same database transaction as the credit, then acknowledge
Acknowledge the message before crediting, so a crash can never lead to the event being delivered again
Check a cache for the event ID before crediting and set it afterwards, using a one-hour TTL on the key

rubric: Recording the ID atomically with the effect makes redelivery harmless.
Cache checks race and expire; ack-first loses credits on crash; a single worker does not stop redelivery.

items.prompt: Plan moving a 5 TB orders table to a new sharded store with zero downtime, where rollback must stay possible at every step until the final cutover. Which sequence satisfies this?

options.label: Backfill history to the new store, switch all traffic, then replay any missed writes from the old store's log
Dual-write to both stores, backfill history, compare shadow reads, switch reads, and retire old writes last
Stop writes, copy the table, switch reads and writes to the new store, then resume traffic
Switch writes to the new store first, then backfill history and migrate reads once the copy completes

rubric: Dual writes keep the old store authoritative and current, so rollback is possible until it is retired.
Other sequences either cause downtime or leave the old store stale.

items.prompt: Design a leaderboard for 50M players (scores 0 to 1,000,000, 200k score updates/s) that returns the top 100 and any player's exact rank within 1 second of a score change. Which design fits?

options.label: Cache each player's rank for one hour by player ID, and recompute the top 100 when the cache entry expires
An hourly batch job that sorts all players and writes ranks into a key-value table for lookups
Sorted sets sharded by score range, with per-shard counts summed to compute a player's exact rank
A single in-memory sorted set on one node, because ranked structures need no partitioning at this scale

rubric: Range sharding spreads the write load while counts give exact ranks quickly.
Caching and batch approaches break the 1-second freshness; one node cannot take 200k updates/s.

items.prompt: A proposed notification design: producers write to a partitioned queue, and a consumer calls an email provider, retrying failures indefinitely in place. Requirement: one malformed message must never delay others in its partition. What is the design missing?

options.label: A cache in front of the email provider, so repeated sends of the same message return a stored response
A synchronous acknowledgement to producers only after the email has actually been delivered to the user
More partitions, so that each message eventually gets its own consumer and cannot block other messages
A bounded retry policy that moves repeatedly failing messages to a dead-letter queue for later inspection

rubric: Infinite in-place retry blocks the partition; bounded retries plus a DLQ isolate poison messages.
More partitions or caching do not stop a poison message blocking its partition.

items.prompt: Design a global read-heavy product catalog: p99 reads under 50 ms worldwide, writes from one region, staleness up to 30 s is fine, and the origin must survive a 10x read spike. Which components together meet this? Select all that apply.

options.label: Synchronous cross-region commit of every catalog write to all replicas
Read replicas in each major region serving local reads
Edge caching with TTLs under 30 seconds for catalog reads
Request coalescing at the cache so concurrent misses trigger one origin fetch
Disabling caching on hot items so they are always read fresh from origin

rubric: Edge TTL caching, regional replicas and coalescing meet latency, staleness and spike limits.
Synchronous global commit is unnecessary given 30 s staleness; uncached hot items overload the origin.

items.prompt: You must design messaging for 10M concurrent connections. Requirements: ordering within each conversation, delivery to offline users when they reconnect, and no message loss after a server crash. Which design meets all three?

options.label: Stateless gateways hold connections; a replicated log partitioned by conversation assigns sequence numbers; clients resume from their last acked sequence
Gateways keep messages in memory per connection and flush to a database each minute, ordering by client timestamps
Pin each conversation to one gateway that holds messages in local memory and replicates them lazily at shutdown
Gateways broadcast every message to all gateways by pub/sub and drop it if the recipient is offline, ordering by arrival time

rubric: A replicated, partitioned log with per-conversation sequence numbers gives ordering, durability and resumable delivery.
Other designs lose messages on crashes or offline users, or order by unreliable timestamps.
